question: Ece texts, “I’m running late for lunch.” What does she mean?
choices: She’ll arrive after the time you agreed.
She has to leave lunch early.
She can only stay for a minute.
She’s already waiting at the table.
note: If you’re running late, you expect to get there later than planned.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: You invite Ali to play football. He replies, “Count me in!” What should you do?
choices: Add him to the list of players.
Ask him to keep the score.
Let him know who wins.
Give him time to decide.
note: “Count me in” is an informal way to say “Yes, I’ll join you.”

question: Your study group meets at four. Jo asks, “Can we bring it forward an hour?” What time does she want to meet?
choices: Three o’clock.
Four o’clock.
Five o’clock.
Six o’clock.
note: Bringing a meeting forward means moving it to an earlier time.

question: Your cousin says, “I’ll pick you up on my way to the match.” What is she offering to do?
choices: Collect you and take you with her.
Save you a seat at the match.
Buy you a ticket on her way.
Meet you when the match ends.
note: If someone picks you up on the way, you travel the rest of the way together.

question: You ask whether to travel on Friday or Saturday. Your friend says, “Let’s leave it open.” What does he want to do?
choices: Decide which day to go later.
Travel on both days.
Call off the trip for good.
Book the Friday trip now.
note: You can leave a date open while you wait to see what works.

picture.alt: A travel suitcase with a blank tag.

question: “Shall we see the horror film?” You’d prefer the comedy and want your friend’s opinion. What do you say?
choices: I’d rather see the comedy. What do you think?
I’m happy with either. You choose.
Let’s get two tickets for the horror film.
I’ve booked the comedy for both of us.
note: “I’d rather” gives your preference. The question leaves the choice open to your friend.

picture.alt: A clapperboard beside a film reel.

question: “I’m at the café by the library. Where are you?” You’re at the one by the station. Ask your friend to stay there while you walk over.
choices: I’m at the other café. Wait there and I’ll come to you.
I’m by the station. Can you come here instead?
I’ll stay where I am. See you in a bit.
Is there a free table at the café by the station?
note: “Wait there” makes it clear who stays. “I’ll come to you” tells your friend who’s moving.

question: A friend needs numbers for dinner tonight. You’d like to come, but you get your work hours at noon. What do you say?
choices: I’d love to. Can I let you know at twelve?
Save me a seat. I’ll be there for sure.
Thanks, but I think I’ll give it a miss.
Twelve is perfect. I’ll meet you there for lunch.
note: “Can I let you know at twelve?” gives your friend a time to expect an answer.

question: Your friend wants to hear the last song. You have ten minutes to catch the last ferry home. What do you say as you leave?
choices: I’d love to stay, but I have to catch my ferry. Enjoy the last song!
I’ll stay for one more. There’s always another ferry.
Let’s see what time the concert ends, then decide.
Shall I wait here while you check the ferry times?
note: The first sentence explains why you’re leaving. “Enjoy the last song!” lets your friend stay.

picture.alt: A ferry beside an İstanbul skyline.

question: “We’re cycling to the lake, then having lunch there.” Your bike is broken. You can take the bus and you’d like to join them for lunch. What do you say?
choices: I’ll skip the ride. Where shall I meet you for lunch?
I’ll ride with you. Can we stop for lunch on the way?
I’ll get my bike fixed and let you know next week.
Enjoy the lake! Let’s have lunch another weekend.
note: “Where shall I meet you for lunch?” accepts the part of the plan you can join.

picture.alt: A bicycle and a pink cycling jersey.

question: On Friday a friend texts, “Tennis next Saturday?” You’re free both weekends, but you’re unsure which day to put in your calendar. What do you ask?
choices: Do you mean tomorrow or the Saturday after?
Would Sunday suit you better than Saturday?
What time on Saturday shall we play?
Shall I book a court for both Saturdays?
note: “Next Saturday” can be understood in two ways. Naming both dates clears it up in one question.

picture.alt: A tennis racket and yellow ball.

question: It’s pouring. You still want to have lunch with your picnic group today. How do you suggest a change of place?
choices: How about bringing the food to my flat instead?
Shall we wait for a sunny weekend?
Could we start our picnic an hour later?
Shall we take the same food next time?
note: “Instead” offers a new place while keeping today’s lunch.

picture.alt: A bowl of salad with croutons.

question: A classmate wants to come to your friend’s board game night. You haven’t asked the host yet. What do you say to the host?
choices: Would it be OK if I brought someone from my class?
I’ve told my classmate there’s room for one more.
Did you enjoy meeting my classmate last time?
Would you like to come to my classmate’s place?
note: “Would it be OK if I brought someone?” gives the host a chance to say yes or no before you invite anyone.

picture.alt: A wooden game piece beside a die.

question: You and a friend are going to a play. She offers to buy both tickets. You’ve already bought yours online. What do you say?
choices: Thanks! Just get yours. I’ve already got mine.
That’s kind of you. I’ll pay you for mine tonight.
Could you get mine too? I’ll buy the drinks.
Shall we buy both tickets at the theatre instead?
note: “Just get yours” saves your friend from buying a ticket you already have.

picture.alt: An empty stage framed by red curtains.

question: Your friend missed last week’s photo walk. You’re going again on Sunday and want to invite her along. What do you say?
choices: I’m going again on Sunday. Do you fancy coming this time?
Did you get any good pictures on last week’s walk?
I’ll send you my favourite photos after Sunday’s walk.
How was your walk? I couldn’t go last Sunday.
note: “Do you fancy coming?” is a friendly invitation. “This time” refers back to the walk she missed.

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.
